**Conventions.** We use the standard definitions.

*Comma category.* For functors $S:\mathbf A\to\mathbf C$ and $T:\mathbf B\to\mathbf C$, the objects of $(S\downarrow T)$ are triples $\langle A,B,f\rangle$ with $A\in\mathbf A$, $B\in\mathbf B$ and $f:SA\to TB$ a morphism of $\mathbf C$. A morphism $\langle A,B,f\rangle\to\langle A',B',f'\rangle$ is a pair $\langle a,b\rangle$ with $a:A\to A'$ in $\mathbf A$ and $b:B\to B'$ in $\mathbf B$ such that $f'\circ Sa=Tb\circ f$. Composition is componentwise, $\langle a',b'\rangle\circ\langle a,b\rangle=\langle a'\circ a,\ b'\circ b\rangle$. The identity on $\langle A,B,f\rangle$ is $\langle\operatorname{id}_A,\operatorname{id}_B\rangle$.

*Slice category.* The objects of $\mathbf C/C$ are the morphisms $g:E\to C$ of $\mathbf C$. A morphism from $g:E\to C$ to $g':E'\to C$ is a morphism $k:E\to E'$ of $\mathbf C$ with $g'\circ k=g$. It is taken with domain $g$ and codomain $g'$. Composition is composition in $\mathbf C$, and the identity on $g:E\to C$ is $\operatorname{id}_E$.

*Category $\mathbf 1$.* It has exactly one object $*$ and exactly one morphism $\operatorname{id}_*$, with $\operatorname{id}_*\circ\operatorname{id}_*=\operatorname{id}_*$.

Here $S=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}$ and $T=F$, where $F*=C$ and $F\operatorname{id}_*=\operatorname{id}_C$.

To show that $J$ is a covariant functor $(\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}\downarrow F)\to\mathbf C/C$, we check four things:
(a) $J$ is defined on every object and sends it to an object of $\mathbf C/C$.
(b) $J$ is defined on every morphism and sends a morphism $X\to Y$ to a morphism $JX\to JY$.
(c) $J$ preserves identities.
(d) $J$ preserves composition.

**(a) Objects.** Let $X$ be any object of $(\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}\downarrow F)$. By definition $X=\langle E,B,g\rangle$ with $E\in\mathbf C$, $B\in\mathbf 1$ and $g:\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}E\to FB$. The only object of $\mathbf 1$ is $*$, so $B=*$. Also $\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}E=E$ and $F*=C$. Hence **every** object has the form $\langle E,*,g\rangle$ with $g:E\to C$ a morphism of $\mathbf C$. So the clause $J\langle E,*,g\rangle=g$ assigns a value to every object, and that value $g:E\to C$ is an object of $\mathbf C/C$.

**(b) Morphisms, domains and codomains.** Let $\langle a,b\rangle:\langle E,*,g\rangle\to\langle E',*,g'\rangle$ be any morphism of $(\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}\downarrow F)$. Then $b:*\to *$ in $\mathbf 1$, and the only such morphism is $\operatorname{id}_*$. Writing $k:=a:E\to E'$, **every** morphism has the form $\langle k,\operatorname{id}_*\rangle$, so the clause $J\langle k,\operatorname{id}_*\rangle=k$ assigns a value to every morphism.

The defining condition of a comma morphism reads
$$g'\circ \operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}(k)=F(\operatorname{id}_*)\circ g .$$
Here $\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}(k)=k$ and $F(\operatorname{id}_*)=\operatorname{id}_C$. Since $g:E\to C$, we have $\operatorname{id}_C\circ g=g$. So the condition becomes
$$g'\circ k=g .$$
This says exactly that $k:E\to E'$ is a morphism of $\mathbf C/C$ from $g$ to $g'$. Thus $J$ sends a morphism $\langle E,*,g\rangle\to\langle E',*,g'\rangle$ to a morphism
$$J\langle E,*,g\rangle=g\ \longrightarrow\ g'=J\langle E',*,g'\rangle,$$
so $J$ preserves domains and codomains.

**(c) Identities.** The identity of $\langle E,*,g\rangle$ in the comma category is $\langle\operatorname{id}_E,\operatorname{id}_*\rangle$. (It is a valid morphism because $g\circ\operatorname{id}_E=g$.) Then
$$J\langle\operatorname{id}_E,\operatorname{id}_*\rangle=\operatorname{id}_E ,$$
and $\operatorname{id}_E$ is the identity morphism of the object $g:E\to C$ in $\mathbf C/C$. Hence
$$J(\operatorname{id}_{\langle E,*,g\rangle})=\operatorname{id}_{J\langle E,*,g\rangle}.$$

**(d) Composition.** Take composable morphisms
$$\langle k,\operatorname{id}_*\rangle:\langle E,*,g\rangle\to\langle E',*,g'\rangle,\qquad \langle k',\operatorname{id}_*\rangle:\langle E',*,g'\rangle\to\langle E'',*,g''\rangle .$$
By part (b), these are general composable morphisms, and $k:E\to E'$, $k':E'\to E''$ satisfy $g'\circ k=g$ and $g''\circ k'=g'$. Composition in the comma category is componentwise, keeping the order of the factors in each component:
$$\langle k',\operatorname{id}_*\rangle\circ\langle k,\operatorname{id}_*\rangle=\langle k'\circ k,\ \operatorname{id}_*\circ\operatorname{id}_*\rangle=\langle k'\circ k,\ \operatorname{id}_*\rangle .$$
The last step uses only the identity law in $\mathbf 1$ in the second component, and leaves the first component $k'\circ k$ unchanged. Therefore
$$J\big(\langle k',\operatorname{id}_*\rangle\circ\langle k,\operatorname{id}_*\rangle\big)=J\langle k'\circ k,\operatorname{id}_*\rangle=k'\circ k .$$
In $\mathbf C/C$, composition is composition in $\mathbf C$, so the composite of $J\langle k,\operatorname{id}_*\rangle=k:g\to g'$ followed by $J\langle k',\operatorname{id}_*\rangle=k':g'\to g''$ is $k'\circ k:g\to g''$. This is a valid slice morphism, since $g''\circ(k'\circ k)=(g''\circ k')\circ k=g'\circ k=g$. Hence
$$J\big(\langle k',\operatorname{id}_*\rangle\circ\langle k,\operatorname{id}_*\rangle\big)=J\langle k',\operatorname{id}_*\rangle\circ J\langle k,\operatorname{id}_*\rangle .$$

**Conclusion.** By (a)–(d), $J$ assigns to each object of $(\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}\downarrow F)$ an object of $\mathbf C/C$. It assigns to each morphism $X\to Y$ a morphism $JX\to JY$, it preserves identities, and it preserves composition in the same order. These are exactly the axioms of a covariant functor, so $J:(\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}\downarrow F)\to\mathbf C/C$ is a covariant functor. $\blacksquare$
